item.title: Italy fines Meta €805 million over unauthorised access to users' photos
item.description: The authority said it reserves the right to conduct a separate investigation into a new feature launched in 2026 that allows content from users' galleries to be processed in the cloud ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: The Italian Data Protection Authority fined Meta Platforms Inc. €805 million ($887 million) for accessing photos and videos of Android users’ galleries without their explicit consent. The company accessed photographs, videos and related metadata stored on Italian users’ smartphones through the Facebook app without obtaining consent and without adequately informing them, the Italian regulator said in a statement Saturday. About 20 million Android users are estimated to have been affected. The authority said it reserves the right to conduct a separate investigation into a new feature launched in 2026 that allows content from users’ galleries to be processed in the cloud. Meta didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. The penalty was imposed on Meta Platforms Ireland Ltd., the company’s main European subsidiary. The size of the fine also takes into consideration a previous 2019 enforcement action against the company, the regulator said. Meta has 60 days to introduce a separate, specific consent request for the feature. The company must also keep the feature disabled by default. The fine is equivalent to about 0.47% of the group’s worldwide revenue, the Italian authority said. (Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)

item.title: Tanker hits cruise ship in New Orleans, 32 hospitalised, none critical
item.description: The cruise ship, which still had about 129 passengers and an unspecified number of crew members aboard, began to sink before tipping over, sending people into the Mississippi River ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Cameron Fozi All passengers and crew members aboard a river cruise ship that capsized after a tanker collision in New Orleans on Friday were accounted for, with 32 people hospitalized but none critically injured, according to Mayor Helena Moreno. The Atlantic Asphalt tanker “lost control” and struck the American Heritage, operated by American Cruise Lines, around 12:30 p.m. at the Port of New Orleans, Moreno said at a news briefing. The cruise ship, which still had about 129 passengers and an unspecified number of crew members aboard, began to sink before tipping over, sending people into the Mississippi River. Harbor police were the first to respond, entering the water to pull people to safety as firefighters extended ladders from the dock. Volunteer crews in their own vessels also joined the rescue effort, Moreno said. “At this moment, the information that we have, we have zero people unaccounted for,” Moreno said. “Which truly is a miracle on the Mississippi.” Video of the incident aired by local television station WDSU, an NBC affiliate, showed a larger tanker approaching the docked cruise ship before the two vessels collided at what appeared to be a relatively slow speed. Later footage showed the American Heritage partly submerged in the river. The American Cruise Lines website describes the American Heritage as a classic paddlewheeler river boat with capacity for as many as 180 passengers, which was last renovated in 2022. “American Cruise Lines can confirm that our riverboat, American Heritage, was involved in a collision while it was docked in New Orleans,” the company said in a statement. “We are in close coordination with the US Coast Guard and local authorities. Guests and crew were evacuated, and we are deeply concerned for everyone involved.” Earlier on Friday, Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry said he was heading to New Orleans. “We are aware of the incident on the Mississippi and we are in close contact with local officials and law enforcement,” Landry said in a post on X. “I am headed to New Orleans now.”

item.title: US transportation secy seeks $50 bn emergency air traffic upgrade funds
item.description: Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the outage was caused by older routers being overloaded with data ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Will Guisbond Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called on Congress to authorize $50 billion in emergency funding to overhaul the US air traffic control system after a technical issue spawned the longest nationwide grounding in more than two decades.  “This is an emergency,” Duffy said at a White House press conference on Friday. He recently asked for about $30 billion to continue funding his agency’s project. “I want Congress to give us emergency funding. This is bipartisan. This is American. I want $50 billion.” Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the outage was caused by older routers being overloaded with data after new software patches were installed throughout the system, but that personnel are still investigating.  It resulted in “intermittent” issues with air traffic control communications, as well as with radar feeds that are used to guide aircraft, Duffy said.  At the beginning of President Donald Trump’s second term, Duffy unveiled a multibillion-dollar plan to modernize and then upgrade the aging ATC infrastructure after a midair collision near Washington killed 67 people in January 2025.  Duffy later that year secured $12.5 billion to kickstart the project, but clinching more funds has proven to be a politically fraught task even considering the issue has bipartisan support. His department wrote a letter, co-signed by the Office of Management and Budget, to re-up a standing $30 billion request this week. So far, the FAA has made progress in modernizing communications lines, radar systems and equipment used by air traffic controllers.  Duffy said the newer equipment installed as a part of his modernization plan was not impacted during the outage, but that more money is needed to build new facilities and completely replace all outdated technology.  Friday’s widespread disruption, which will take days for airlines to recover from, is one of several that have beset the nation’s aviation system in recent years. However, only the multi-day fallout from the Sept. 11, 2001 terrorist attacks resulted in a grounding longer and more disruptive than this one.  The failure Friday evokes recent memories of chaos in September when a fiber optic cable was cut by construction crews, triggering a cascading havoc that hit airports across the Northeast.  In 2023, a relatively brief outage of the FAA’s safety notification system for pilots and dispatches resulted in a 90-minute nationwide grounding.

item.title: Listing may change 'Tata way', put profits ahead of philanthropy: Noel
item.description: Noel said while 'some people' are proposing a listing for group's holding company, he fears that enlarging the number of shareholders after a listing will shift its focus to profits from philanthropy ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / Companies / News / Listing may change 'Tata way', put profits ahead of philanthropy: Noel

Listing may change 'Tata way', put profits ahead of philanthropy: Noel Noel said while 'some people' are proposing a listing for group's holding company, he fears that enlarging the number of shareholders after a listing will shift its focus to profits from philanthropy

The comments come at a time when ruptures at the top echelons of the country's largest conglomerate are out in the open | Image: Bloomberg

Press Trust of India New Delhi 6 min read Last Updated : Nov 14 2026 | 3:41 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Tata Trusts Chairman Noel Tata on Saturday expressed concern that a proposed public listing of Tata Sons could fundamentally alter the group's traditional business philosophy, warning that a wider shareholder base may eventually place profits ahead of philanthropy.   "My worry is that listing, which is what some people are proposing, will change the Tata way. And one day, if we have 30,000-40,000 shareholders, profit may take precedence over philanthropy. And I think that will fundamentally change the Tata way of working," Noel Tata said at the HT Leadership Summit 2026.   He said Tata Trusts would work with regulators and other stakeholders to find a solution that preserves the group's founding ethos.

"Tata Trusts will play a constructive role with regulators and others to try and find a solution which keeps the Tata way the way it is," he said.   The remarks come against the backdrop of an intensifying tussle between Tata Trusts and the Tata Sons board over the holding company's ownership structure and leadership. Tata Trusts, which controls about 66 per cent of Tata Sons - the holding company of the $165 billion Tata Group - has opposed a public listing, while the Shapoorji Pallonji Group, its second-largest shareholder with an 18.37 per cent stake, has backed a stock market float to unlock value from its investment.

The dispute gained momentum after the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) rejected Tata Sons' September 2026 application to surrender its registration as a core investment company, effectively closing a route the group had pursued to avoid mandatory listing as an upper-layer non-banking financial company.   At a September 17 board meeting, Tata Sons decided to initiate steps towards listing in line with RBI regulations and approved a fresh five-year term for Chairman N Chandrasekaran, reversing his August decision not to seek reappointment after February 2027.   Noel Tata opposed both decisions, with the Trusts subsequently questioning the legality of Chandrasekaran's reappointment. The board approved his reappointment by a 4:1 vote.

Emphasising continuity in the group's philosophy, Noel on Saturday said its ownership structure and institutional character had helped preserve its values across generations.   "The owner cannot die, the owner cannot be bought and the owner cannot retire. There is continuity in what happens the Tata way," he said.   The group has historically combined commercial operations with philanthropy and nation-building, with Tata Trusts playing a central role in its institutional framework.   On the group's strategic direction, Noel said there was no question about its broad objectives, but greater discipline was needed in executing large projects and allocating capital.   "Philanthropy on one hand. Nation building on the other. This is independence of leadership and personalities and this will continue. I do not question the direction of what we have done. I question, sometimes, the delivery of what we are doing," he said.

"The question is, do we have the discipline when we execute projects, and not the direction? How will projects with a long gestation period succeed if we don't have discipline? And how will we allocate capital to those projects?" he said.   "So, very clearly, the direction is fine, but we also need discipline in the execution of these very large projects," he added.   Highlighting the group's role in India's industrial development, Noel said Tata companies were participating in emerging sectors such as semiconductors and electric vehicle batteries.   "We are partners in India's development," he said, adding that the group was undertaking its first semiconductor project and setting up its first EV battery plant.

Noel also spoke about the growth of Tata's retail business, particularly Trent, which operates the Westside and Zudio brands.   He said Zudio was launched in 2016 to cater to consumers at the bottom of the economic pyramid by offering aspirational products at affordable prices.   "It was not that this aspiration for better product was only in the top metros or with the wealthy. The aspiration went down all the way. So we said, how can we address in a way the bottom of the pyramid? So in 2016, we launched Zudio to address this bottom of the pyramid with an aspirational product," he said.

The format started with air-conditioned stores of around 6,000 square feet, with prices beginning at ₹199, he said, adding that the starting price point had remained unchanged over the past decade.   On Westside, Noel said the decision to adopt a private-label model gave the company control over the entire value chain, from fabric and product design to retailing.   He said Westside, which began with doubts over whether such a retail format could succeed in India, now operated around 320 stores and was looking at expanding to more than 500.   Attributing the growth partly to rising consumption, he said demand had increased across socio-economic categories and markets over the past decade.

Noel also said the opportunity to address the needs of underserved sections of society had made a deep impression on him after taking over as chairman of Tata Trusts, adding that the experience had given him greater humility about the scale of social challenges in India.   Tata Trusts vice-chairman Venu Srinivasan and other trustees backing a stock market listing of Tata Sons are understood to favour greater transparency, stronger corporate governance and a clearer ownership structure for India's largest business conglomerate.   They argue that listing would subject the holding company to greater public and regulatory scrutiny, institutionalise decision-making and reduce uncertainty over succession and governance in a group whose businesses span multiple sectors. A public listing could also provide a market-determined valuation of Tata Sons and give investors greater visibility into the financial and strategic decisions of the group.

In a November 11 letter to fellow trustee Darius Khambata, Srinivasan and fellow vice-chairman Vijay Singh cited examples such as Novo Nordisk, Hershey, Lundbeck and Demant to argue that companies can remain anchored by charitable foundations while being publicly traded.   They also pointed to listed Tata companies, including TCS, Tata Steel, Tata Power and Tata Motors, which have undertaken long-gestation investments and nation-building projects without compromising their institutional character.   The Trusts would continue to retain their shareholding in Tata Sons and receive dividends to fund philanthropic activities, they argued, adding that greater disclosure would bring discipline rather than constrain the group's long-term ambitions.
